resources.string: Get the free Windows / Mac receiver

Use the receiver’s IPv4 address and port (normally 42734). Windows supports a virtual Xbox controller with its free driver. Mac maps sticks, triggers and buttons to keyboard/mouse controls; it does not create a native gamepad or preserve analog trigger pressure. Use Player 1 on Mac. Full setup: Support → PC.

string-array.item: Aim and drive with one finger

string-array.name: help_tour_bodies
string-array.item: Build a controller around the movements that feel comfortable. Buttons, sticks and touchpads can share a profile. Use Next or swipe the picture to browse this short tour. You can reopen it from Support.

Open Bridge menu and choose Practice. Nothing is sent to a game. Try a game starter, touch a button and move a stick. Release all stops phone actions. Pages keep related controls together inside one profile.

Auto-center returns a stick to the middle when you lift. Turn it off to keep moving without holding your finger down; use Re-center to stop. Stick+ adds actions at chosen distances, such as running farther out and jumping at the edge. Assignments depend on your game.

A Button Aim control can hold aim while your drag moves the right stick. Add fire to the same control for a combined pad. A driving pad can hold the trigger while left and right movement steers. You choose the actions and trigger amounts.

Hold Toggle keeps an action down after a long touch. Repeat taps it for you. Macro Mode finishes a timed sequence from one tap. Touch Aim can choose stages from finger contact size on supported phones; a normal aiming pad is an alternative that needs no contact calibration.

Tap Edit, drag a control, then save. Hold a control in Edit to change its size and actions. Use small circles where comfortable. Keep frequent actions close to your finger and use pages for other controls. Profiles and backups let you keep different setups.

No Pico or adaptive controller is needed for Windows or Mac. Install and run the free receiver on the computer, then use the same home network. Choose Windows / Mac receiver and type its IPv4 address and port. Windows offers a virtual controller; Mac maps your controls to keyboard and mouse. Support has the full steps.

Console play needs a separate compatible adaptive controller and bridge device. Go to the Support tab to find links to the GitHub connections. The documented Pico W route uses an Xbox Adaptive Controller. Check the PlayStation section before buying hardware; that route is not the same.

resources.string:
1. Download PC-Receiver.zip from your app’s GitHub Releases page and extract the whole folder on the computer. No Pico or adaptive controller is needed.

2. On Windows: follow the receiver guide to install its free virtual-controller driver and run Setup-Windows-Receiver.bat. Start-Windows-Receiver.bat starts play.

On Mac: install Python 3.10 or newer if needed, then open Start-Mac-Receiver.command. Follow its Accessibility permission instructions in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility. Restart the receiver after granting access. No virtual-controller driver is used.

3. Put the phone and computer on the same trusted home network. Leave the receiver open and read its IPv4 address and port (normally 42734). Use the computer’s local address, not the phone’s address or an internet address. Allow receiver access on your private network if the firewall asks.

4. Open connection settings, choose Windows / Mac receiver, enter that IP and port, then connect. Use Player 1 on Mac.

5. Windows sends gamepad, keyboard and mouse inputs. Mac sends keyboard and mouse inputs: by default the left stick is WASD, the right stick moves the pointer, LT is right click and RT is left click. Buttons map to common keys; edit the receiver’s mapping file to match your game. Mac does not create a native gamepad: movement keys are digital and trigger pressure becomes pressed/released. Games must accept keyboard/mouse input.

6. Test in an empty document first on Mac, or the controller test panel on Windows. Confirm each action releases, then press Release all. Open the game and match its keyboard/mouse or controller bindings. Keep the receiver open while playing.

Mac uses one shared keyboard and mouse, not separate controllers for two players. Do not expose the receiver’s port to the internet. Support links below include exact setup and troubleshooting.

Xbox: use a Raspberry Pi Pico W or Pico WH with the phone bridge firmware, an Xbox Adaptive Controller, a data-capable micro-USB cable and the controller’s documented external power supply. The original Pico without W and Pico 2 W are not interchangeable with this firmware.

The phone and Pico use the same home network. Connect the phone Pico to the Adaptive Controller’s left USB port. The setup guide explains firmware, IP address and SCX2 settings, plus the Xbox X1/X2 mapping used for full-press LT/RT. USB full-press mode does not supply partial trigger pressure.

A separate Pico W can turn a compatible Permobil Omni2 Bluetooth mouse joystick into the right stick. Read the chair bridge guide before pairing. Existing switches can remain connected directly to the adaptive controller.

PlayStation: the current Pico-to-Xbox-Adaptive-Controller route does not directly connect to a Sony Access controller. An appropriate console-compatible adapter route is needed and has not been verified by this project. Check the FAQ and the adapter maker’s current requirements before buying or connecting anything.

Replay the picture tour, watch the silent beginner videos or read the setup FAQ. The videos demonstrate the iPhone app; Android has many matching controls but its menus and available options can differ.\n\nStart in Practice, change one control at a time and save a backup before experimenting. If a held action surprises you, use Release all. Opening Support releases phone actions without changing your saved profiles or receiver settings.
